# Unit 5: Nursing management of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders

This unit covers INC Unit V (10 hours). Schizophrenia is the prototype psychotic disorder and a cornerstone of the whole subject. Understand the biology, recognise the symptoms, know the antipsychotic drugs and their side effects, and be confident with nursing diagnoses and care plans.

---

## 5.1 Review: What is a psychotic disorder?

A **psychotic disorder** is characterised by a loss of contact with reality — the person cannot tell what is real from what is not. The defining features are **hallucinations** (false perceptions) and **delusions** (fixed false beliefs), and in schizophrenia, also **disorganised thinking** and **negative symptoms**.

## 5.2 Schizophrenia: overview and epidemiology

- Prevalence: approximately 1% of the world population; affects all cultures.
- Onset: typically late teens to mid-30s; males tend to present earlier (early 20s) than females (late 20s).
- Course: episodic with incomplete remission (many patients have residual symptoms between episodes); a minority recover fully; some deteriorate.
- Schizophrenia is a leading cause of long-term disability worldwide.

## 5.3 Aetiology and dopamine hypothesis

No single cause is established; schizophrenia is best explained by a **biopsychosocial model**.

| Factor | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Genetic | Twin studies: 50% concordance in identical twins; 10–15% in first-degree relatives (vs ~1% general population) |
| Neurodevelopmental | Prenatal events (maternal infection, malnutrition, hypoxia); minor brain structure differences |
| Neurotransmitter | Dopamine hypothesis: excess dopaminergic activity in mesolimbic pathway → positive symptoms; hypodopaminergia in prefrontal cortex → negative symptoms |
| Glutamate | NMDA receptor hypofunction also implicated |
| Psychosocial | High expressed emotion in family, urban living, social adversity can trigger relapse |
| Substance use | Cannabis use (especially adolescent onset) is a risk factor |

**Dopamine hypothesis in brief:**

```text
  MESOLIMBIC pathway overactive → POSITIVE symptoms (hallucinations, delusions)
  MESOCORTICAL pathway underactive → NEGATIVE symptoms (flat affect, poverty of speech)
  NIGROSTRIATAL pathway blocked by drugs → EXTRAPYRAMIDAL side effects
  TUBEROINFUNDIBULAR pathway blocked → HYPERPROLACTINAEMIA
```

## 5.4 Types of symptoms

### Positive symptoms (added to normal experience)

| Symptom | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Hallucinations | Auditory most common: third-person commentary, voices discussing the patient, command hallucinations |
| Delusions | Persecutory, grandiose, reference, passivity (thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting/control) |
| Disorganised speech | Loosening of associations, tangentiality, incoherence, word salad |
| Disorganised behaviour | Unpredictable, socially inappropriate actions; catatonia |

### Negative symptoms (taken away from normal experience)

| Symptom | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Affective flattening | Reduced range and intensity of emotional expression |
| Alogia | Poverty of speech; brief, empty replies |
| Avolition | Lack of motivation to initiate or sustain activity |
| Anhedonia | Inability to feel pleasure |
| Social withdrawal (asociality) | Loss of interest in social contact |
| Attentional impairment | Difficulty focusing on tasks |

Negative symptoms are more difficult to treat and are most responsible for long-term disability.

### Cognitive symptoms

Impaired working memory, attention, executive function and processing speed — present before the first episode and persist throughout.

## 5.5 Subtypes of schizophrenia (DSM-IV; still asked in exams)

| Subtype | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| Paranoid | Prominent delusions and/or hallucinations; relatively preserved functioning |
| Disorganised (hebephrenic) | Disorganised speech and behaviour, flat or inappropriate affect; poor prognosis |
| Catatonic | Marked psychomotor disturbance — stupor, negativism, rigidity, waxy flexibility, excitement |
| Undifferentiated | Criteria for schizophrenia met but not fitting one specific subtype |
| Residual | No prominent positive symptoms but negative symptoms and mild positive features persist |

(Note: DSM-5 removed formal subtypes from the diagnostic criteria but they remain in teaching and older INC references.)

## 5.6 Other psychotic disorders

| Disorder | Key features |
| --- | --- |
| **Brief psychotic disorder** | Psychotic symptoms lasting 1 day to 1 month, then full recovery; often after stress |
| **Schizophreniform disorder** | Same features as schizophrenia but lasting 1–6 months |
| **Schizoaffective disorder** | Schizophrenia symptoms PLUS major mood episode (depression or mania) occurring together and at different times |
| **Delusional disorder** | Fixed, non-bizarre delusion; functioning otherwise relatively preserved; no prominent hallucinations |
| **Substance-induced psychosis** | Psychotic symptoms caused directly by a substance (cannabis, amphetamine) or its withdrawal (alcohol) |
| **Psychosis due to medical condition** | Systemic lupus, thyroid disorders, delirium, epilepsy, etc. |

## 5.7 Assessment of a patient with schizophrenia

**MSE findings typically seen in schizophrenia:**
- Appearance: dishevelled, poor hygiene
- Behaviour: disorganised, catatonic posturing or agitated
- Speech: poverty of speech or disorganised; echolalia; neologisms
- Mood: flat or blunted affect; incongruent affect (laughing while expressing a sad thought)
- Thought form: loosening of associations, tangentiality, thought blocking
- Thought content: persecutory, reference, passivity delusions
- Perception: auditory hallucinations (third-person, commanding, arguing voices)
- Cognition: impaired attention and concentration
- Insight: Grade 1 or 2 in acute phase
- Judgement: impaired

**Diagnostic criteria (ICD-10 simplified):** At least one clear first-rank symptom (or two second-rank) for at least one month, not explained by organic illness or substances.

Schneider's **first-rank symptoms** (highly characteristic of schizophrenia):
- Thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting
- Passivity feelings (made feelings, made impulses, made actions)
- Delusional perception
- Third-person auditory hallucinations (voice commentary, two voices discussing)

## 5.8 Medical management

**First-line:** Atypical antipsychotic (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) for 2 or more years after first episode.

**Second-line:** Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed two adequate antipsychotic trials).

**Adjuncts:** Benzodiazepine in acute agitation; mood stabiliser in schizoaffective disorder.

**Acute phase care:** May need involuntary admission under MHCA 2017 if patient is dangerous or unable to care for themselves; manage agitation safely.

**Maintenance:** Long-acting injectable antipsychotics for poor adherence.

## 5.9 Nursing diagnoses and care

### Common nursing diagnoses

1. Disturbed sensory perception (auditory/visual hallucinations)
2. Disturbed thought processes (delusional thinking)
3. Risk for violence (self-directed or other-directed)
4. Self-care deficit (bathing, grooming, feeding, toileting)
5. Impaired social interaction
6. Disturbed sleep pattern
7. Non-compliance with medication
8. Ineffective coping
9. Deficient knowledge (patient and family about illness and treatment)

### Nursing interventions

**For hallucinations:**
- Do not argue with or deny the hallucinations but do not reinforce them: "I know the voices are real to you, but I am not hearing them."
- Help the patient identify when hallucinations are worst (triggers: stress, fatigue, isolation).
- Offer distraction (music through headphones, activity, conversation).
- Assess for command hallucinations instructing harm; report at once.
- Ensure medicines are given and taken (observe swallowing).

**For delusions:**
- Do not argue, agree, or challenge the delusional belief directly.
- Do not play along ("That must be terrible to have people following you") — this reinforces the belief.
- Redirect to reality-based topics calmly.
- Document the content precisely using the patient's words.
- Assess whether the delusion poses a risk to self or others.

**For disorganised behaviour:**
- Keep the environment calm and predictable with clear structure.
- Use short, simple sentences.
- Break tasks into small steps.
- Anticipate needs rather than waiting for the patient to become agitated.

**For self-care deficit:**
- Assist with hygiene, dressing, meals and toileting without taking over.
- Provide prompts and step-by-step guidance.
- Use positive reinforcement; never mock or shame.

**For risk of violence:**
- Monitor for warning signs: pacing, clenched fists, raised voice, intense staring.
- De-escalate early: calm tone, personal space, offer choice ("Would you like to walk with me?").
- Remove potential weapons from the environment (sharps, breakable objects).
- Call for help before the patient becomes unmanageable.
- Document all incidents and near-misses.

**For medication non-adherence:**
- Educate about the importance of maintenance therapy.
- Identify reasons for stopping (side effects, lack of insight, stigma, cost).
- Address side effects proactively (e.g. use depot injection for forgetting; anticholinergic for EPS).
- Involve family in supervision of medications.

### Safety considerations

- **Ligature points:** assess the ward environment; remove cords, belts, extension cables from areas accessible to suicidal patients.
- **Absconding:** know the patient's level of leave and supervise accordingly.
- **Self-neglect:** some patients may not eat, drink or manage fluid balance.

## 5.10 Health education for patient and family

| Topic | Key messages |
| --- | --- |
| Nature of illness | Schizophrenia is a brain illness, not a moral failure or spiritual problem; it is treatable |
| Medicines | Take every day, even when feeling well; never stop suddenly; report side effects |
| Early warning signs | Sleep disturbance, increasing suspicion, hearing voices — come back to clinic early |
| Stress | High stress and high expressed emotion can trigger relapse; keep life stable |
| Substances | Avoid cannabis and alcohol — these make symptoms worse and cause relapse |
| Follow-up | Regular clinic visits; crisis plan if relapse begins |
| Stigma | Help family understand and explain to neighbours; rights under MHCA 2017 |

## 5.11 Application and implication in nursing

- Always document the content of delusions and hallucinations exactly — this helps track improvement.
- Reward reality-based interaction; build on healthy parts of the person's functioning.
- Engage the family as partners; reducing expressed emotion reduces relapse rates.
- Recovery is possible; hold hope even when the patient cannot.

## Remember

- Schizophrenia: onset 18–35 years; affects 1% of population; genetic risk in first-degree relatives ~10–15%.
- Positive symptoms: hallucinations (auditory most common), delusions (persecutory, passivity), disorganised speech and behaviour.
- Negative symptoms: flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal — harder to treat.
- Dopamine hypothesis: mesolimbic excess → positive symptoms; mesocortical deficit → negative symptoms.
- Schneider's first-rank symptoms include thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, passivity phenomena, third-person hallucinations.
- Subtypes: paranoid (best prognosis), hebephrenic/disorganised (worst), catatonic, undifferentiated, residual.
- Schizoaffective = schizophrenia features + major mood episode.
- Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day–1 month then full recovery.
- Nursing: do not argue with delusions or deny hallucinations; use short sentences; supervise self-care; monitor for violence warning signs; educate family about expressed emotion and early warning signs.
- Clozapine: treatment-resistant schizophrenia; weekly WBC monitoring mandatory.

# Unit 6: Nursing management of mood disorders

This unit covers INC Unit VI (10 hours). Mood disorders — depression and bipolar disorder — are among the most common, most disabling and most treatable of all psychiatric conditions. Suicide risk assessment runs through every section. This is a high-scoring unit.

---

## 6.1 Overview of mood disorders

**Mood disorders** are characterised by a primary, clinically significant disturbance of mood — either low (depression), high (mania), or both at different times (bipolar disorder). They cause marked distress and impaired functioning.

```text
  SPECTRUM OF MOOD
  ←─────────────────────────────────────────────────────→
  Severe      Moderate   Mild      Euthymia    Hypomania   Mania
  Depression  Depression Depression (normal)   (mild high)  (severe high)
```

## 6.2 Depression: types and classification

| Type | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| Major depressive disorder (MDD) | One or more major depressive episodes; most common diagnosis |
| Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) | Low-level, chronic depression lasting at least 2 years |
| Postpartum (postnatal) depression | Onset within 4 weeks (up to 1 year) after childbirth |
| Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) | Depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern (usually winter) |
| Premenstrual dysphoric disorder | Severe mood changes in the week before menstruation |
| Psychotic depression | Major depression with delusions or hallucinations (mood-congruent) |
| Recurrent depressive disorder | Multiple episodes, with normal mood between episodes |

## 6.3 Clinical features of depression

### Diagnostic criteria (simplified DSM-5/ICD-10)

For a major depressive episode: **five or more** of the following symptoms, present for at least **two weeks**, including either (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest/pleasure:

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Depressed mood | Sad, empty, hopeless; tearfulness; in some patients irritability |
| Loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia) | Cannot enjoy activities that were once pleasurable |
| Weight change | Significant weight loss or gain; change in appetite |
| Sleep disturbance | Insomnia (most common) or hypersomnia |
| Psychomotor change | Retardation (slowed movement, speech) or agitation |
| Fatigue | Low energy nearly every day |
| Worthlessness/guilt | Excessive, inappropriate guilt; self-blame |
| Cognitive impairment | Reduced concentration, indecisiveness |
| Suicidal ideation | Recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, plan or attempt |

### Beck's cognitive triad

Aaron Beck described the negative thinking pattern of depression as three interlocking negative beliefs:

```text
  BECK'S COGNITIVE TRIAD:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. Negative view of SELF              │
  │     "I am worthless, a failure"        │
  │                                        │
  │  2. Negative view of the WORLD         │
  │     "Everything is against me"         │
  │                                        │
  │  3. Negative view of the FUTURE        │
  │     "Nothing will ever get better"     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

These thinking patterns are the target of cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT).

### Biological features ("somatic" or "vegetative" symptoms — especially examined)

- **Early morning awakening** (wakes 2–3 hours earlier than normal; cannot return to sleep) — classic
- Mood worse in the morning (diurnal variation — improves slightly during the day)
- Marked weight loss and appetite loss
- Markedly decreased libido
- Psychomotor retardation

## 6.4 Aetiology of depression

| Factor | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Genetic | Twin concordance; family history doubles risk |
| Neurobiological | Monoamine hypothesis: deficiency of serotonin and/or noradrenaline; HPA axis dysregulation (cortisol excess) |
| Psychological | Beck's cognitive model (learned negative thinking); learned helplessness (Seligman) |
| Life events | Loss (bereavement, job, relationship), trauma, chronic stress are precipitants |
| Medical | Hypothyroidism, Cushing's, cancer, stroke, Parkinson's disease, chronic pain |
| Drugs | Corticosteroids, beta-blockers, reserpine, oral contraceptives |
| Social | Social isolation, poverty, domestic violence |

## 6.5 Suicide: assessment and nursing care

Suicide is a major risk in depression. All depressed patients must be assessed for suicide risk.

### Why depressed patients are at risk

- Hopelessness is the strongest predictor (even more than depression severity).
- Early in recovery (when energy improves before mood fully lifts) is a particularly dangerous time.
- Late evening and early morning are higher-risk periods.

### Risk assessment

```text
  Assess: Ideation → Plan → Intent → Means available
  "Are you having thoughts that life is not worth living?"
  "Have you thought about how you might do it?"
  "Have you taken any steps?"
```

| High-risk features | Low-risk features |
| --- | --- |
| Previous attempt | No previous attempt |
| Specific, lethal plan | No specific plan |
| Access to means (medication, weapon) | No access to means |
| Male sex, older age | Female sex, younger age |
| Social isolation, no support | Strong social support |
| Hopelessness, intent to die | Ambivalence, reason for living |
| Alcohol or drug use | No substance use |
| Recent discharge from hospital | Community contact maintained |

### Nursing care for the suicidal patient

- **Never leave the patient alone** when suicidal risk is assessed as high.
- Remove all potential means from the environment (medications, sharps, belts, cords, breakable glass).
- Carry out **safety contract** (ask patient to agree not to act on suicidal thoughts without informing staff) — note: this is a clinical tool, not a legal safeguard.
- Do not make false promises of confidentiality; suicidal plans must be shared with the team.
- Establish a therapeutic relationship: listen empathically without minimising.
- Increase observation level as ordered (15-minute, 30-minute or continuous special).
- Notify the physician and document fully.
- Provide psychoeducation to family about warning signs and safe storage of medications.
- After a suicidal attempt: post-attempt care — medical treatment of injuries, psychological assessment, do not leave alone.

**Warning signs of imminent suicide:**
- talks about suicide or death
- gives away prized possessions
- says goodbye to people, ties up affairs
- sudden calmness after a period of severe depression (may have made a decision)

## 6.6 Management of depression

### Pharmacotherapy (reviewed briefly here; full detail in Unit 4)

| Class | First choice | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSRI | Fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram | First-line; safe in overdose |
| SNRI | Venlafaxine, duloxetine | For depression with pain |
| TCA | Amitriptyline, imipramine | Effective but dangerous in overdose (cardiac) — caution in suicidal patients |
| MAOI | Phenelzine | Used rarely; dietary tyramine restriction |
| Mirtazapine | Mirtazapine | Useful when sleep and appetite loss are prominent |

**Key nursing point:** Antidepressants take 2–4 weeks; warn patient not to stop early because they "feel nothing is happening." Close monitoring in the first 2 weeks of a new prescription.

### Psychotherapy

- **CBT** — first-line for mild-to-moderate depression; targets Beck's cognitive triad.
- **Interpersonal therapy (IPT)** — focuses on relationships and social roles.
- **Behavioural activation** — schedule pleasant activities; overcomes withdrawal.

### ECT for depression

Fastest and most effective treatment for severe depression with:
- suicidal risk so high the patient cannot wait for drugs
- refusal to eat or drink (risk of physical deterioration)
- severe psychotic depression
- failure to respond to two or more adequate drug trials
- severe depression in pregnancy (avoid drugs)

(Procedure and nursing care: see Unit 4.)

## 6.7 Nursing care in depression

| Problem | Nursing interventions |
| --- | --- |
| Low mood and anhedonia | Accept feelings without minimising; encourage small pleasures; behavioural activation |
| Self-neglect | Assist with hygiene and meals; offer preferred foods; nutritional assessment |
| Sleep disturbance | Sleep hygiene; warm milk, relaxation; avoid caffeine and screens |
| Psychomotor retardation | Gentle encouragement; keep tasks very simple; do not rush |
| Suicidal ideation | (See 6.5 above) constant vigilance, observation, remove means |
| Non-adherence | Education about delayed onset; involve family; simplify regimen |
| Social withdrawal | Gradually increase social contact; group activities |
| Hopelessness | Help identify reasons for living; set tiny, achievable goals |

**Nurse's self-care:** Working with depressed and suicidal patients is emotionally draining. Seek supervision; recognise vicarious trauma.

## 6.8 Bipolar disorder

**Bipolar disorder** is characterised by episodes of mania (or hypomania) alternating with episodes of depression, with periods of relatively normal mood (euthymia) in between.

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Bipolar I | At least one full manic episode (may also have depressive episodes) |
| Bipolar II | Recurrent depressive episodes + hypomania (not full mania) |
| Cyclothymia | Numerous periods of hypomanic and mild depressive symptoms over at least 2 years |
| Rapid cycling | Four or more mood episodes in 12 months |

### Features of mania (the manic episode)

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Elevated or irritable mood | Euphoric, expansive, or intensely irritable |
| Grandiosity | Inflated self-esteem; belief in special powers, wealth, identity |
| Decreased need for sleep | Rested after 3 hours; does not feel tired |
| Pressured speech | Rapid, loud, difficult to interrupt |
| Flight of ideas | Racing thoughts; jumps from one topic to another |
| Distractibility | Attention drawn easily by irrelevant stimuli |
| Increased goal-directed activity / psychomotor agitation | Many projects, hypersexuality, overspending |
| Reckless behaviour | Excessive spending, risky sexual behaviour, dangerous driving, unwise business decisions |
| Psychotic features (in severe mania) | Grandiose or persecutory delusions, hallucinations |

A **manic episode** lasts at least 1 week. **Hypomania** is similar but less severe and shorter (at least 4 days); does not cause marked impairment or require hospitalisation.

### Management of mania

**Acute:**
- **Hospitalisation** often needed (poor insight, impulsive behaviour, dangerous spending or sexual behaviour).
- **Mood stabilisers:** lithium, sodium valproate, carbamazepine (onset takes 1–2 weeks).
- **Atypical antipsychotics:** olanzapine, quetiapine — fast sedation and control of agitation.
- **Benzodiazepines:** short-term for agitation and sleep.

**Maintenance (prevention of further episodes):**
- Lithium is the gold standard for bipolar prevention; also reduces suicide risk.
- Sodium valproate, lamotrigine (especially for bipolar depression).
- Psychoeducation and mood charting.

### Nursing care in mania

| Problem | Interventions |
| --- | --- |
| Hyperactivity and poor rest | Low-stimulation environment; structured timetable; encourage sleep and rest |
| Nutritional deficit (too busy to eat) | Finger foods, frequent snacks; high-calorie drinks |
| Impulsive, reckless behaviour | Limit access to phone, credit cards, car keys; set firm limits consistently |
| Grandiosity and poor insight | Do not challenge beliefs aggressively; redirect, set limits, give information |
| Pressured speech | Remain calm; use brief, clear responses; allow venting to a limited extent |
| Hypersexuality | Private room if possible; redirect; protect other patients; non-judgemental manner |
| Risk of exhaustion or medical complications | Monitor vitals, hydration, nutrition, skin, joints; encourage rest between activities |
| Non-adherence (doesn't believe ill) | Education; involve family; depot or supervised meds; explain consequences |

## 6.9 Postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis

| Condition | Onset | Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baby blues | Days 3–5 | Tearfulness, anxiety, mood swings; self-limiting | Reassurance, support |
| Postpartum depression | Within 4 weeks to 1 year | Low mood, anhedonia, guilt, fear of harming baby, bonding difficulty | SSRI, psychotherapy, support |
| Postpartum psychosis | Within 2 weeks | Delusions, hallucinations, severe agitation, confusion; psychiatric emergency | Hospitalisation, antipsychotic, mood stabiliser; protect baby |

**Nursing priority in postpartum psychosis:** assess risk to the baby — command hallucinations to harm the baby require immediate action; protect the infant.

## 6.10 Seasonal affective disorder (SAD)

- Depressive episodes occur at the same time each year, typically autumn/winter.
- Features: increased sleep, increased appetite (carbohydrate craving), weight gain, fatigue, low mood.
- Management: **light therapy** (bright-light lamp 10,000 lux for 30 minutes in the morning), SSRI antidepressants, CBT.
- Remits spontaneously in spring.

## Remember

- Major depressive episode: five features for ≥2 weeks; must include depressed mood or anhedonia.
- Beck's cognitive triad: negative view of self, world and future — target for CBT.
- Biological features of depression: early morning awakening, diurnal variation (worse in AM), weight loss, decreased libido, psychomotor retardation.
- Suicide risk: assess ideation → plan → intent → means; hopelessness is the strongest predictor; previous attempt is the biggest risk factor.
- Antidepressants take 2–4 weeks; monitor for suicidal ideation in early weeks; TCAs are dangerous in overdose.
- ECT: fastest for severe depression with suicidal risk or refusal to eat.
- Mania: elevated/irritable mood, grandiosity, reduced sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, impulsive reckless behaviour.
- Bipolar I: full manic episode; Bipolar II: hypomania + depression.
- Lithium: gold standard for bipolar prevention; narrow therapeutic window; monitor levels; dehydration raises levels.
- Postpartum psychosis: psychiatric emergency within 2 weeks of birth; protect the baby.
- SAD: winter depression; treat with morning bright-light therapy.

# Unit 7: Nursing management of neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders

This unit covers INC Unit VII (10 hours). These disorders are very common in the community and in general hospital settings. The nurse meets them on every ward, not just in a psychiatric unit. Understanding anxiety and somatisation is therefore a core nursing competency.

---

## 7.1 Overview: neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders

The term **neurosis** refers historically to mental disorders without a break with reality (unlike psychosis). The major groups in this unit are:

```text
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ANXIETY DISORDERS                                          │
  │  Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)                        │
```

## 7.2 Normal anxiety versus pathological anxiety

**Anxiety** is an unpleasant emotional state of apprehension and tension, often in response to a vague or unknown threat. Normal anxiety is protective and motivating. Pathological anxiety is:
- excessive or out of proportion to the situation
- persistent and difficult to control
- causing significant distress or impaired functioning

### Levels of anxiety (Peplau)

| Level | Features | Nurse's role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild (+) | Increased alertness; better learning and problem-solving | Use this — it facilitates coping |
| Moderate (++) | Narrowed focus; selective inattention; some impairment | Redirect attention; stay calm; offer simple guidance |
| Severe (+++) | Greatly narrowed focus; physical symptoms; can focus on only one specific detail | Direct, simple instructions; remain with the patient |
| Panic (++++) | Loss of control; terror; fight or flight; may harm self | Stay with patient; calm environment; medication if ordered; never leave alone |

### Physical manifestations of anxiety

Anxiety activates the **sympathetic nervous system** (fight-or-flight response):

| System | Symptoms |
| --- | --- |
| Cardiovascular | Palpitations, tachycardia, chest pain, raised BP |
| Respiratory | Shortness of breath, hyperventilation, chest tightness |
| Gastrointestinal | Nausea, diarrhoea, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing |
| Musculoskeletal | Trembling, muscle tension, fatigue, restlessness |
| Neurological | Headache, dizziness, tingling, feeling faint |
| Other | Sweating, flushing, frequent urination, sleep disturbance |

## 7.3 Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)

- **Features:** excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple topics for ≥6 months; associated with restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.
- **Aetiology:** genetic predisposition, overactive amygdala, stressful life events, personality.
- **Management:** CBT (most effective long-term), relaxation training, buspirone, SSRI/SNRI.
- **Nursing care:** therapeutic relationship; teach relaxation techniques (progressive muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing, guided imagery); help patient identify worry triggers; support problem-solving.

## 7.4 Panic disorder

- **Panic attack:** a sudden, intense episode of overwhelming fear with physical symptoms (palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, sweating, trembling, fear of dying or losing control) peaking within 10 minutes.
- **Panic disorder:** recurrent, unexpected panic attacks + persistent concern about further attacks or change in behaviour to avoid them.
- Panic attacks are **not dangerous** (no cardiac events) but are terrifying.
- **Management:** SSRI (first-line long-term); CBT with interoceptive exposure; benzodiazepine short-term for acute attacks.

**Nursing care during a panic attack:**
- Stay with the patient — do not leave.
- Calm, matter-of-fact tone: "You are having a panic attack; it will pass in a few minutes; you are not dying."
- Help the patient breathe more slowly — guide diaphragmatic breathing (breathe in through nose for 4 counts, hold for 2, out through mouth for 4).
- Do not ask many questions; keep the environment quiet.
- After the attack, teach panic management techniques.

## 7.5 Phobias

A **phobia** is a marked, persistent, excessive and unreasonable fear of a specific object, activity or situation that leads to avoidance and causes impaired functioning.

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Specific phobia | Fear of a specific stimulus: blood, spiders, heights, flying, injections |
| Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) | Intense fear of social situations; embarrassment; avoidance of social contact |
| Agoraphobia | Fear and avoidance of situations where escape is difficult (open spaces, crowds, public transport); often accompanies panic disorder |

**Management:**
- **Systematic desensitisation:** gradual, graded exposure to the feared stimulus while maintaining relaxation (Wolpe).
- **In-vivo exposure/flooding:** exposure to the feared stimulus at full intensity (less comfortable; more rapid results).
- **Cognitive restructuring:** challenge irrational beliefs about the feared stimulus.
- SSRI for social phobia and panic.

**Nursing care:**
- Do not force the patient into the feared situation.
- Teach relaxation; practise before graded exposure.
- Give positive reinforcement for each step in desensitisation.
- Educate about the nature of phobias and that avoidance maintains fear.

## 7.6 Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)

- **Obsessions:** recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges that the patient recognises as their own (unlike thought insertion in schizophrenia) and tries to suppress or neutralise.
- **Compulsions:** repetitive behaviours or mental acts the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession, to reduce anxiety or prevent a dreaded event. The person knows they are excessive.
- Common obsession–compulsion pairs: contamination (washing); doubt (checking locks, switches); order (arranging symmetrically); harm (checking one has not harmed others); religious or sexual thoughts (praying, counting).

**Nursing care:**
- Do not stop compulsive rituals abruptly — this causes severe anxiety.
- Do not participate in rituals or reassure rituals.
- Structure daily schedule to allow reduced ritual time gradually (ERP programme under psychologist).
- Provide a calm, predictable environment.
- Encourage CBT with **exposure and response prevention (ERP)** — the most effective psychological treatment.
- Clomipramine (TCA) or SSRI (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline) are first-line pharmacotherapy.

## 7.7 Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

- **Cause:** exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — either directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about happening to a close person.
- **Features:** symptoms in four clusters:

```text
  PTSD FOUR SYMPTOM CLUSTERS:
  1. RE-EXPERIENCING   Flashbacks, nightmares, psychological and physical distress
                       on reminders
  2. AVOIDANCE         Avoiding thoughts, feelings, reminders of trauma
  3. NEGATIVE COGNITIONS/MOOD  Distorted blame, negative emotions, diminished
                               pleasure, detachment
  4. HYPERAROUSAL      Sleep difficulty, irritability/anger outbursts, recklessness,
                       hyper-vigilance, startle response, concentration difficulty
```

- **Duration:** symptoms for more than 1 month after the trauma.
- **Management:** **Trauma-focused CBT** or **EMDR** (Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing) are first-line; SSRI.

**Nursing care:**
- Build trust slowly; never force disclosure of the traumatic event.
- Provide safety, stability, predictability.
- Teach grounding techniques (focus on the present moment using the five senses) for flashbacks.
- Identify triggers and help patient manage them.
- Educate family about PTSD symptoms; they may misread hypervigilance as aggression.

## 7.8 Somatoform disorders

**Somatoform disorders** are characterised by physical symptoms that cannot be fully explained by a medical condition, substance or another mental disorder, and that are linked to psychological factors or conflicts. The patient genuinely experiences the symptoms.

| Disorder | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Somatisation disorder** | Multiple physical complaints in multiple body systems over years; not explained medically; causes impaired functioning and health-seeking |
| **Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)** | Neurological symptoms — paralysis, blindness, seizures, aphonia — without neurological disease; often begins after stress; "la belle indifférence" (apparent calm about disability) |
| **Hypochondriasis (illness anxiety disorder)** | Persistent preoccupation with having a serious illness; misinterprets normal body sensations; not reassured by medical investigation |
| **Pain disorder** | Chronic pain for which psychological factors play a major role in onset, severity or maintenance |
| **Body dysmorphic disorder** | Preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in physical appearance |

**General nursing principles for somatoform disorders:**
- Accept that the patient's distress and disability are real, even if no organic cause is found.
- Do not dismiss or argue ("it's all in your head").
- Build a stable, trusting therapeutic relationship.
- Schedule regular, brief appointments (not on demand — reduces reinforcement of sick-role behaviour).
- Avoid excessive investigation and procedures; each investigation reinforces preoccupation.
- Gradually shift focus from symptoms to function ("Can we focus on what you can do today?").
- Treat concurrent depression and anxiety (often present).
- Psychoeducation: explain the mind-body connection without dismissal.
- Refer to liaison psychiatry in general hospital settings.

## 7.9 Dissociative disorders

**Dissociation** is a disruption in the integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity or perception. It is usually a defence response to overwhelming trauma.

| Disorder | Feature |
| --- | --- |
| Dissociative amnesia | Inability to recall important personal information (usually traumatic); not due to brain injury |
| Dissociative fugue | Purposeful travel away from home with amnesia; sometimes assumption of a new identity; rare |
| Depersonalisation/derealisation | Feeling detached from one's own body (depersonalisation) or the surrounding world (derealisation) |
| Dissociative identity disorder (DID) | Presence of two or more distinct personality states, each with its own pattern of perceiving and relating |

**Nursing care:**
- Provide safety and a stable environment; do not challenge the dissociation directly.
- Avoid confrontation about identity states.
- Refer for specialist trauma therapy.
- Manage concurrent suicide risk.

## 7.10 General nursing principles for anxiety and neurotic disorders

| Principle | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Establish therapeutic alliance | Calm, non-judgemental presence; listen first |
| Assess severity and risk | Use anxiety scales; ask about suicide risk |
| Provide psychoeducation | Explain that anxiety is a normal biological response; it will not harm them |
| Teach relaxation techniques | Progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, guided imagery — practise with the patient |
| Reinforce healthy coping | Identify what the patient already does that helps |
| Limit environmental stimulation | Quiet room, low lighting, calm voice |
| Involve the family | Teach family not to provide excessive reassurance (reinforces avoidance) |
| Encourage physical activity | Regular exercise reduces anxiety and depression |
| Monitor medication | Benzodiazepines only short-term; warn about dependence |
| Coordinate with therapy | Reinforce CBT homework; support exposure plans |

## 7.11 Application and implication in nursing

- In a general hospital ward, every patient admitted for a physical complaint may have anxiety or somatisation. Screen and refer early.
- Nurses with high expressed empathy but no professional boundary can overinvolve themselves with somatising patients — seek supervision.
- Trauma-informed care applies to all nursing settings, not just psychiatric wards.

## Remember

- Peplau's anxiety levels: mild, moderate, severe, panic — nursing response increases with severity.
- Panic attacks: 10 minutes to peak; not dangerous; stay with patient, guided breathing, reassure.
- Phobias: systematic desensitisation (gradual exposure + relaxation) is the treatment.
- OCD: obsessions are ego-dystonic (patient knows they are excessive); compulsions reduce anxiety; treatment = ERP + SSRI/clomipramine; never stop rituals abruptly.
- PTSD: four clusters — re-experiencing, avoidance, negative cognitions, hyperarousal; >1 month after trauma; treatment = trauma-focused CBT or EMDR.
- Somatoform disorders: physical symptoms not explained by organic cause; accept patient's distress; avoid excessive investigation; focus on function; CBT.
- Conversion disorder: neurological symptoms without neurological disease; "la belle indifférence."
- Dissociation: disruption of consciousness/memory/identity, usually after trauma; provide safety, refer for trauma therapy.
- General anxiety nursing: psychoeducation, relaxation techniques, CBT reinforcement, avoid excessive reassurance, short-term benzodiazepines only.
